Megiddo
Megiddo guarded the pass into the Jezreel Valley; kings fought there in Deborah's song, and King Josiah fell there in battle against Pharaoh Necho.
Revelation gathers the kings of the whole world to the place called in Hebrew Armageddon, often understood as 'mountain of Megiddo', though Megiddo is a mound, not a mountain.
Megiddo was a fortified city layered with some twenty levels of occupation. Whether Armageddon means Megiddo, Mount Carmel nearby, or a symbolic 'mount of assembly' is debated.
Mount Carmel
On Carmel Elijah challenged the prophets of Baal, and fire fell from heaven to show who was the true God.
Revelation's beast from the land makes fire come down from heaven to deceive, a dark mirror of Carmel, and Elijah's ministry lies behind the two witnesses.
The Carmel ridge runs towards the coast above the Jezreel Valley and Megiddo. Some interpreters link the 'mountain' of Armageddon with Carmel.
Jerusalem and Mount Zion
David made Jerusalem his capital and Solomon built the temple there; it was destroyed by Babylon, rebuilt after the exile, and was the city where Jesus was crucified and raised.
The Lamb stands on Mount Zion with the 144,000, the earthly city where the Lord was crucified is trampled, and the book ends with the new Jerusalem coming down from heaven.
Jerusalem's temple was destroyed by Babylon in 586 BC and by Rome in AD 70. Interpreters disagree whether some of Revelation's judgements refer to the city's fall in AD 70.
Bethlehem
Bethlehem was the home of Ruth and the birthplace of David, and Micah foretold that a ruler would come from there; Jesus was born there.
Revelation 12 shows a woman giving birth to a male child who will rule the nations while a dragon waits to devour him, a heavenly view of the nativity and Herod's threat.
Bethlehem lies about nine kilometres south of Jerusalem. The Church of the Nativity stands over a cave venerated since at least the second century.
Tyre
Tyre was the great Phoenician sea-trading city; Isaiah and Ezekiel announced its fall and pictured its merchants and sailors mourning over it.
Revelation 18's lament for Babylon, with its cargo list and weeping kings, merchants and sailors, is modelled closely on Ezekiel's dirge over Tyre.
Tyre was an island city until Alexander the Great built a causeway to capture it in 332 BC. Its purple dye and shipping made it a byword for wealth.
Nineveh
Nineveh, capital of Assyria, repented at Jonah's preaching but later fell in 612 BC, as Nahum foretold.
Nahum calls Nineveh a harlot and mistress of sorceries whose fall makes onlookers clap, language that Revelation reuses for Babylon.
Nineveh lies across the Tigris from modern Mosul in Iraq. Its palaces held the library of Ashurbanipal and the reliefs of Sennacherib's siege of Lachish.
Babylon under Nebuchadnezzar destroyed Jerusalem and the temple and carried Judah into exile; Daniel served there, and Jeremiah and Isaiah foretold its fall.

Revelation's Babylon the great is the proud city that persecutes the saints and seduces the nations; most read it as Rome, some as Jerusalem, some as a future city, and the call to 'come out of her' quotes Jeremiah.
Babylon lay on the Euphrates south of modern Baghdad. Cyrus of Persia took it in 539 BC, partly by diverting or wading the river, a memory Revelation's drying of the Euphrates may echo.
River Euphrates (near Carchemish)
The Euphrates marked the northern limit of the land promised to Abraham, and at Carchemish on its banks Babylon defeated Egypt in 605 BC.
In Revelation four angels bound at the great river Euphrates are released, and the sixth bowl dries up the river to prepare the way for the kings from the east.
For Rome the Euphrates was the frontier with the feared Parthian cavalry. Interpreters debate whether Revelation's Euphrates is literal or a symbol of invasion from beyond the empire's edge.
The Kebar canal near Nippur
Among the exiles by the Kebar canal, Ezekiel saw the heavens opened and the throne-chariot of God with four living creatures, a rainbow and wheels full of eyes.
Revelation's throne room, living creatures, rainbow, sealed scroll eaten by the prophet, measured temple and river of life all draw heavily on Ezekiel.
The Kebar is usually identified with the naru kabaru, a canal near Nippur known from Babylonian tablets, though the exact course is uncertain.
Susa
Susa was a Persian royal city where Daniel saw his vision of the ram and the goat, Nehemiah served the king, and Esther saved her people.
Daniel's visions of beasts and horns, received in the Persian and Babylonian courts, supply Revelation's beast imagery and its pattern of a people kept safe under hostile empire.
Susa, in south-west Iran, was the winter capital of the Persian kings; Darius I built a great palace there.
Damascus
Abraham's servant Eliezer came from Damascus, the city was capital of Aram in the days of the kings, and Saul met the risen Christ on the road there.
Damascus is not named in Revelation, but Paul's conversion vision of the glorified Jesus anticipates John's vision of the risen Christ in Revelation 1.
Damascus is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, set in an oasis fed by the Barada river.
Bozrah in Edom
Isaiah pictures the Lord coming from Edom, from Bozrah, in garments stained red because he has trodden the winepress of his wrath alone.
Revelation's rider on the white horse wears a robe dipped in blood and treads the winepress of the fury of God's wrath, drawing directly on Isaiah 63.
Bozrah is identified with Buseirah in southern Jordan, an Edomite capital of the Iron Age. Edom in prophecy often stands for the nations hostile to God's people.
Alexandria
Alexandria is mentioned in Acts as the home of Apollos and of grain ships that carried Paul; there the Hebrew Scriptures were translated into Greek.
Revelation does not name Alexandria, but its Greek Old Testament wording and the grain ships of Revelation 18's cargo trade belong to the Mediterranean economy Alexandria fed.
Founded by Alexander in 331 BC, Alexandria became the Ptolemaic capital, home of the great library and the Septuagint translation, and Rome's chief grain port.
Antioch on the Orontes
In Antioch believers were first called Christians, and from there Paul and Barnabas were sent out on their missionary journeys.
Antioch is not named in Revelation, but it was the Seleucid capital of Antiochus IV, whose persecution in Daniel 7-11 shaped the image of a blasphemous beast and a time, times and half a time.
Antioch, modern Antakya in Turkey, was the third city of the Roman empire and the base of the Roman governor of Syria.
Rome
Paul wrote to the church in Rome and later arrived there as a prisoner; Christian tradition holds that Peter and Paul died there under Nero.

Most interpreters see Rome behind Babylon the great, the city on seven hills ruling the kings of the earth and drunk with the blood of the saints, while others read Babylon as Jerusalem or a future world city.
Rome was famously built on seven hills. Nero's persecution after the fire of AD 64 and the later imperial cult form the background against which many read Revelation.
The Mediterranean ("the sea")
For Israel 'the Great Sea' was the western boundary of the land and a place of storms and danger, as Jonah and Paul both found.
The beast rises out of the sea, the merchants and sailors lament Babylon from the sea, and in the new creation there is no more sea.

Rome called the Mediterranean 'our sea'; its shipping lanes carried the empire's goods and armies. Seen from Patmos, the beast's rising from the sea suggests power arriving from Rome across the water.
Patmos
John was on the island called Patmos because of the word of God and the testimony of Jesus when he received the revelation.
Revelation was seen on Patmos and sent from there to seven churches on the mainland of Asia.

Patmos is a small rocky island in the Aegean, and Roman authorities used such islands for banishment. John's exile is dated either under Nero (late 60s) or, following Irenaeus, under Domitian (about AD 95).
Paul spent about three years in Ephesus, where the riot over Artemis broke out; Timothy later led the church there.
The risen Christ praises Ephesus for testing false apostles but rebukes it for leaving its first love, and promises the tree of life in God's paradise.
Ephesus was the chief city of Roman Asia and home of the great temple of Artemis. Its harbour was steadily silting up, and it held a provincial temple of the emperors from the time of Domitian.
The church in Smyrna is not described in Acts; it later became known for its bishop Polycarp, martyred there around AD 155.
The letter to Smyrna promises the crown of life to those faithful unto death and warns of ten days of tribulation and slander.

Smyrna, modern Izmir, prided itself on long loyalty to Rome and won the right to build a temple to Tiberius in AD 26. The city had been rebuilt after centuries in ruins, matching Christ's title as the one who died and came to life.
Pergamum's church held firm even when Antipas, Christ's faithful witness, was killed there.
Christ says Pergamum is where Satan's throne is, warns against the teaching of Balaam, and promises hidden manna and a white stone with a new name.

Pergamum had the great altar of Zeus, a famous shrine of Asclepius, and in 29 BC became the first city in Asia with a temple to Augustus and Roma. Which of these 'Satan's throne' refers to is debated.
Lydia, the seller of purple goods whom Paul met in Philippi, came from Thyatira.
The letter to Thyatira warns against 'Jezebel', who leads servants into sexual immorality and idol food, and promises authority over the nations and the morning star.
Thyatira, modern Akhisar, had many trade guilds of dyers, bronze-smiths and others, whose feasts honoured patron gods and put pressure on Christians who worked in those trades.
Sardis is not mentioned outside Revelation in the New Testament.
Christ tells Sardis it has a name for being alive but is dead, urges it to wake up, and warns he will come like a thief; the faithful few will walk in white.

Sardis, the old Lydian capital of Croesus, had an acropolis thought impregnable, yet it was taken by surprise at night by Cyrus and again by Antiochus III. It was badly damaged in the earthquake of AD 17.
Philadelphia is not mentioned outside Revelation in the New Testament.
Christ holds the key of David and sets an open door before Philadelphia, promising to make the one who conquers a pillar in God's temple who will never go out, bearing a new name.

Philadelphia, modern Alaşehir, suffered repeated earthquakes after AD 17, and many residents lived outside the city for fear of falling buildings. It took the new name Neocaesarea in thanks for imperial relief.
Paul mentions the church at Laodicea and a letter sent to it, linking it with nearby Colossae and Hierapolis.
Christ calls Laodicea lukewarm, neither hot nor cold, and urges the self-satisfied church to buy gold, white garments and eye salve; he stands at the door and knocks.

Laodicea was a rich banking and textile city famed for black wool and an eye remedy, and it rebuilt after the AD 60 earthquake without Roman help. Its water came by aqueduct from springs to the south near modern Denizli and arrived tepid and mineral-laden, unlike the hot springs of Hierapolis or the cold water of Colossae.
Hierapolis
Paul notes that Epaphras laboured hard for the believers in Laodicea and Hierapolis.
Hierapolis is not named in Revelation, but many interpreters think its hot springs, seen across the valley from Laodicea, lie behind the contrast of hot, cold and lukewarm in the letter to Laodicea.
Hierapolis, modern Pamukkale, is famous for hot mineral springs and white travertine terraces. Tradition links it with the apostle Philip, and Papias was its bishop in the early second century.
Colossae
Paul wrote to the church at Colossae, founded through Epaphras, and asked that his letter be read in Laodicea too.

Colossae is not named in Revelation; its cold, fresh water is often contrasted with Laodicea's lukewarm supply in reading Revelation 3, and Colossians' hymn of Christ as the beginning of creation parallels Revelation 3:14.
Colossae lay in the Lycus valley about 16 kilometres east of Laodicea. Its mound has never been fully excavated, though survey work began in the 2010s.
Abraham's journey

Abram leaves Ur with his father, settles in Haran, then goes on at God's call into Canaan; Damascus marks the usual route south and Jerusalem stands for the land of promise, where Melchizedek of Salem blessed him. Hebrews says he was looking for the city with foundations that Revelation shows coming down.
The Exodus

Israel is freed from Egypt through the plagues and the Passover lamb, meets God at Sinai, and enters the land at Jericho with seven trumpets. The route and Sinai's location are debated; Revelation retells this story with the Lamb, the plagues and the song of Moses.
Into exile

Nebuchadnezzar takes Judah's people from Jerusalem to Babylon, and by the Kebar canal Ezekiel sees the throne of God among the exiles. Revelation's throne vision is born from this memory of God present in a foreign land.
The return from Babylon

After Cyrus's decree in 538 BC, exiles return to rebuild Jerusalem and its temple, travelling up the Euphrates and south through Syria rather than across the desert. Isaiah's call to go out of Babylon becomes Revelation's 'Come out of her, my people'.
The circuit of the seven letters

The seven churches lie on a roughly circular Roman road, and a messenger landing at Ephesus from Patmos would reach them in exactly this order, as William Ramsay observed. Whether John chose the order for this reason is likely but not certain.
From Babylon to Rome

Babylon destroyed Jerusalem's temple in 586 BC and Rome destroyed it again in AD 70, so Jewish and Christian writers came to call Rome 'Babylon', as 1 Peter appears to do. Revelation 17-18 uses the name for the great city, which most read as Rome, though some argue for Jerusalem or a future city.
